body:
The East India Company enters Indian politics

The English East India Company originally came to India primarily for trade. During the 18th century, competition for commercial privileges, control of trading settlements and political influence increasingly involved the Company in military conflicts.

Two victories before 1761 are particularly important: Plassey in Bengal in 1757 and Wandiwash in southern India in 1760. Both strengthened British influence, but the opponents and immediate results were different.

Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757

The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 at Palashi, or Plassey, in Bengal.

  • Company side: East India Company forces commanded by Robert Clive.
  • Opposing side: The forces of Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal.
  • Result: Victory for the East India Company.

The immediate dispute concerned Company privileges, interference in Bengal's politics and the strengthening of Company fortifications. A major reason for the Nawab's defeat was the failure of troops under Mir Jafar, one of his commanders, to fight for him. Clive had secured Mir Jafar's support by promising to make him Nawab.

After the victory, Siraj-ud-Daulah was killed and Mir Jafar became Nawab of Bengal. The Company gained substantial political influence. Plassey was its first major military victory in India, although it did not immediately give the Company direct control over the entire subcontinent.

Battle of Wandiwash, 22 January 1760

The Battle of Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760 at Vandavasi in present-day Tamil Nadu. It was part of the Third Carnatic War between British and French forces in India.

  • British side: East India Company forces commanded by Eyre Coote.
  • French side: Forces commanded by Count de Lally.
  • Result: British victory.

Wandiwash severely weakened French military power in southern India and helped the British gain an advantage over their principal European commercial rival.

The essential difference

Plassey was fought against the Nawab of Bengal. Its importance lay in the Company's growing influence over the politics and resources of Bengal. Wandiwash was fought against French forces. Its importance lay in the British victory over a European rival during the Carnatic conflict.

Neither battle should be confused with the Third Battle of Panipat. The British East India Company was not one of the 2 principal opposing sides at Panipat in 1761.

Prelims focus

  • Plassey, 23 June 1757: Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah.
  • Mir Jafar: His failure to support the Nawab contributed to the defeat at Plassey.
  • Wandiwash, 22 January 1760: Eyre Coote defeated French forces commanded by Count de Lally.
  • Location: Plassey is in Bengal; Wandiwash is in present-day Tamil Nadu.
  • Trap: Plassey was not a battle between the British and French. Wandiwash was.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory: The Company Establishes Power, printed pp. 12–14, 2020–21 edition; Royal Collection Trust, Map of the Battle of Wandiwash, 1760, Collection Reference RCIN 733001, historical description, consulted 19 November 2026.]
title: Plassey (1757) and Wandiwash (1760): Two Different British Victories

body:
Why the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali fought

By the middle of the 18th century, the Mughal Empire had lost much of its effective power. The Marathas had expanded their influence into northern India, while Ahmad Shah Abdali, also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani, led an Afghan power that also sought influence in the region.

The conflict arose from competition for political and military control in northern India, including the area around Delhi. The Maratha advance also created opposition among some regional rulers who feared the extension of Maratha power.

Date, place and opposing armies

The Third Battle of Panipat took place on 14 January 1761 near Panipat in present-day Haryana.

Maratha side

The Maratha field army was commanded by Sadashivrao Bhau. It represented a major northern expedition of the Maratha power. Balaji Baji Rao was the Peshwa at the time, but he was not the commander leading the Maratha army on the battlefield.

Afghan and allied side

The opposing coalition was led by Ahmad Shah Abdali or Durrani. It included:

  • Rohilla Afghan forces, including those associated with Najib-ud-Daulah.
  • Shuja-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Awadh.

These Indian allies mattered because the conflict was not simply a confrontation between a foreign Afghan army and an otherwise united India. Regional political interests shaped the opposing alliances.

Outcome and significance

Ahmad Shah Abdali's coalition won. The Maratha army suffered a devastating defeat, including the loss of important commanders and a very large number of soldiers. The battle is remembered as one of the most destructive military confrontations of the 18th century.

The defeat seriously weakened the Maratha position in northern India and interrupted its expansion. It also demonstrated that the authority of the Mughal emperor no longer determined who controlled the region.

What the battle did not mean

The Third Battle of Panipat did not immediately end Maratha power everywhere in India. Maratha political and military strength recovered in subsequent years, although the scale and consequences of the 1761 defeat were severe.

Nor was Panipat a victory won by the East India Company. British influence was expanding through separate developments, including victories at Plassey and Wandiwash, but the principal combatants at Panipat were the Marathas and the coalition led by Abdali.

Prelims focus

  • Date: 14 January 1761.
  • Maratha commander: Sadashivrao Bhau.
  • Opposing leader: Ahmad Shah Abdali, also called Ahmad Shah Durrani.
  • Abdali's Indian allies: Rohilla forces, including Najib-ud-Daulah, and Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh.
  • Result: Abdali's coalition defeated the Marathas.
  • Trap: The British East India Company was not the victor at Panipat, and the defeat did not permanently eliminate every centre of Maratha power.

[Sources: Panipat District Administration, Third Battle of Panipat (1761), consulted 19 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, printed pp. 149–151, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, printed p. 18, 2020–21 edition.]

body:
How the major battles fit into Indian history

The decisive battles between 1526 and 1761 belong to several different phases. Babur's campaigns established and consolidated Mughal rule. Humayun's defeats and Akbar's recovery of Delhi show how that rule was challenged and restored. Talikota and Haldighati involved major regional powers. Samugarh was part of an internal Mughal succession struggle. During the 18th century, regional states, foreign invaders and European trading companies competed for influence as Mughal authority weakened.

Chronological reference

The following table brings together the year, principal opposing sides and immediate result of each major battle covered in this lesson.

Battle and yearPrincipal opposing sidesImmediate result
First Panipat, 1526Babur and Ibrahim LodiBabur won; Lodi rule at Delhi ended.
Khanwa, 1527Babur and Rana Sanga's coalitionBabur won.
Chanderi, 1528Babur and Medini RaiBabur captured Chanderi.
Ghaghra, 1529Babur and eastern Afghan opponentsBabur won.
Chausa, 1539Sher Khan and HumayunSher Khan won.
Kannauj, 1540Sher Shah and HumayunSher Shah won; Humayun lost his kingdom.
Second Panipat, 1556Akbar's forces and HemuAkbar's forces won.
Talikota, 1565Deccan Sultanate coalition and VijayanagaraSultanate coalition won.
Sarnal, 1572Akbar and Ibrahim Husain MirzaAkbar won.
Haldighati, 1576Man Singh's Mughal army and Maharana PratapMughal battlefield advantage; Pratap remained free.
Bhuchar Mori, 1591Mughal Gujarat and Muzaffar Shah III's coalitionMughal forces won.
Dharmat, 1658Aurangzeb and Murad versus imperial forcesAurangzeb and Murad won.
Samugarh, 1658Aurangzeb and Murad versus Dara ShikohAurangzeb and Murad won.
Khajwa, 1659Aurangzeb and Shah ShujaAurangzeb won.
Jajau, 1707Prince Muazzam and Azam ShahMuazzam won.
Palkhed, 1728Baji Rao I and Nizam-ul-MulkMaratha victory.
Karnal, 1739Nadir Shah and Muhammad Shah's forcesNadir Shah won.
Plassey, 1757Robert Clive and Siraj-ud-DaulahEast India Company won.
Wandiwash, 1760Eyre Coote's British forces and Count de Lally's French forcesBritish victory.
Third Panipat, 1761Ahmad Shah Abdali's coalition and the MarathasAbdali's coalition won.

The 3 Battles of Panipat compared

All 3 battles took place in the Panipat region, but they were separated by long intervals and involved different political struggles.

BattleYearMain distinction
First Panipat1526Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi and began Mughal rule at Delhi.
Second Panipat1556Akbar's forces defeated Hemu and secured the restored Mughal position.
Third Panipat1761Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas.

Anniversaries in the news during 2026

Historical anniversaries are calculated from the year or date of the original event. A commemoration may make a battle prominent in current affairs, but it does not change the historical record of the battle.

500 years since the First Battle of Panipat

The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526. Its 500th anniversary fell on 21 April 2026. The Council on Foreign Relations identified the 500th anniversary of the establishment of Mughal rule as a notable anniversary for 2026 in an article published on 2 December 2025.

450 years since the Battle of Haldighati

The Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576. Its 450th anniversary fell on 18 June 2026. A report published by The Times of India on 17 June 2026 discussed preparations in Rajasthan to mark the anniversary. A subsequent report published by Udaipur Kiran on 20 June 2026 described commemorative activities at Haldighati.

These are reports concerning the 2026 anniversary period. The information above is stated at the 19 November 2026 content cutoff. The historical dates remain 1526 and 1576 irrespective of the commemorations.

Keeping anniversaries distinct

The Battle of Khanwa took place in 1527, so its 500th anniversary falls in 2027, not 2026. Similarly, the Third Battle of Panipat took place in 1761, so its 250th anniversary was in 2011, not 2026.

Four distinctions that prevent common errors

  • First Panipat and Khanwa: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and Rana Sanga at Khanwa.
  • Second Panipat and Haldighati: Hemu opposed Akbar's forces at Panipat in 1556; Maharana Pratap opposed Man Singh's Mughal army at Haldighati in 1576.
  • Samugarh and Karnal: Samugarh was a Mughal succession battle in 1658; Karnal was a Persian invasion battle in 1739.
  • Plassey, Wandiwash and Third Panipat: The East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey, British forces defeated the French at Wandiwash, and Abdali's coalition defeated the Marathas at Panipat.

Prelims focus

  • Three Panipats: 1526, 1556 and 1761.
  • Three key leaders: Babur at Khanwa; Rama Raya at Talikota; Aurangzeb at Samugarh.
  • Gujarat: Sarnal in 1572; Mughal subah established in 1573; Bhuchar Mori in 1591.
  • 2026 anniversaries: 500 years since First Panipat and 450 years since Haldighati.
  • Trap: A battlefield victory does not always imply complete or permanent political control, as the aftermaths of Haldighati, Talikota and Third Panipat demonstrate.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapters 4 and 10, The Mughal Empire and Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part II, Class 12, Theme 7; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2; Panipat District Administration, First, Second and Third Battles of Panipat, consulted 19 November 2026; Council on Foreign Relations, Ten Anniversaries to Note in 2026, published 2 December 2025; The Times of India, Maharana Pratap Circuit Yet to Take Shape as Haldighati Marks 450 Years, published 17 June 2026; Udaipur Kiran, Haldighati Marks Maharana Pratap Jayanti and 450th Shaurya Diwas, published 20 June 2026; Ahmedabad University, Bhuchar Mori seminar description, 26 March 2025.]
